findings: Single lateral radiograph of a flexed elbow (flexion appears greater than the canonical ~90 degrees) extending through the forearm (radius and ulna) toward a partially cropped wrist. Across 6 independent first-pass reviews and 6 independent image-inspection reviews (15 image-level reports covering the original plus 9 derived visualizations), cortical margins of the humerus, radius, and ulna were consistently described as continuous, with no fracture line, displaced fragment, cortical step-off, dislocation, or focal destructive lesion identified in any image. A faint anterior soft-tissue (fat-pad) shadow adjacent to the distal humerus was noted on both the original and the locally-contrast-enhanced (CLAHE) elbow crop, without elevation or a discrete 'sail sign'; no posterior fat pad was identified. A pixel-intensity histogram of the bright proximal joint region showed 0.00% of pixels clipped at maximum value, indicating the region's contrast enhancement reflects recoverable underlying signal rather than fabricated detail. Edge-enhancement processing (full-shaft and a zoomed pass targeting the radial neck/coronoid/olecranon) repeatedly produced candidate linear features at the radial-head/coronoid and radius/ulna overlap zone; four independent reviewing agents applied a mandatory cross-check against the unprocessed original and each independently reclassified these as normal anatomic superimposition in this projection, not confirmed fracture lines. A heuristic (non-validated, image-statistics-based) alignment-line overlay showed the estimated capitellum position close to the forearm-axis line without a clear malalignment signal, though the atypical flexion angle limits confidence in this check. The small carpal/wrist bone cluster visible at the inferior edge of the frame is incompletely imaged (cropped) and is non-diagnostic beyond showing no gross fracture in the small portion visible.
impression: This AI research-pipeline synthesis found no fracture, dislocation, or focal destructive lesion on this single lateral elbow/forearm view; the study appears grossly unremarkable across all independent reviews performed. This is not a clinical radiological diagnosis and must not be used for clinical decision-making.
limitations: Only one projection is available; a true fracture/alignment assessment normally requires at least one orthogonal (AP) view, which was not provided, so a subtle or non-displaced fracture (especially at the elbow) cannot be fully excluded. The wrist/carpal region and proximal humerus are cropped/incompletely included, and no laterality marker, patient identifier, or acquisition metadata is visible. All reviewing agents in this pipeline are independent instances of the same underlying model (Claude Sonnet 5, run six times in parallel for the first-pass review and six more times for image inspection); their mutual agreement reflects consistency across independent runs of one model architecture, not independent cross-model or clinical validation, and must not be treated as diagnostic confirmation. Several candidate features produced by contrast and edge-enhancement processing were identified by multiple independent reviewers as processing or projection artifacts (CLAHE noise/texture amplification, unsharp-mask overlap-boundary lines) rather than true pathology; all derived images are supporting visualizations of the same original pixel data, not new diagnostic information. This entire analysis is a university research/testing exercise on multi-agent LLM image-analysis pipelines and is not a substitute for professional radiological interpretation; any real clinical concern should be evaluated by a qualified clinician with appropriate imaging.
